question: How do four hands keep a simple melody distinct from its surrounding harmony?
intro: Ravel opens his five children’s pieces with a slow pavane for Sleeping Beauty, played here on one piano by four hands. This complete miniature is the only movement from the duet suite in this selection.

sections.label: Opening · lower and upper phrases
sections.mNote: The lower part begins; the upper part adds its melody.

sections.label: Middle · connected phrases
sections.mNote: A more continuous line moves through the middle register.

sections.label: Return · upper phrase
sections.mNote: The earlier upper melody returns and settles into the close.

cues.title: One piano, four hands
cues.text: The lower player begins alone. The upper part first answers briefly, then introduces a higher melody over repeated accompanying notes. Listen for the change of register without imagining a second instrument: both players share the same piano and its resonance.
cues.evidence: Durand 1910 piano-duet score, printed pp. 2–3: Seconda begins alone; Prima has two bars of rest, a brief answer in bar 3 and a higher phrase from bar 5. https://hdl.handle.net/1802/17620. No exact entry timestamp is assigned.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Children and a fairy tale
cues.text: Ravel dedicated Ma mère l’Oye to Mimie and Jean Godebski. The opening piece takes its Sleeping Beauty from Charles Perrault’s fairy tale. Its modest scale is deliberate: this is one of five children’s pieces for piano duet, not a miniature reduction of the later orchestral ballet.
cues.evidence: IRCAM work catalogue identifies the dedication and original five-piece piano-duet version: https://brahms.ircam.fr/fr/work/ma-mere-l%27oye (page HTML). Literary source and later versions: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ma_m%C3%A8re_l%27Oye. The 1910 score is explicitly for piano four hands.

cues.title: Young pianists at the premiere
cues.text: The first public performance was given by Jeanne Leleu and Geneviève Durony, aged eleven and fourteen, at the Salle Gaveau on 20 April 1910. The dedication to children was matched by young performers, though they were not the two Godebski children named in the score.
cues.evidence: IRCAM work catalogue, premiere fields and commentary in page HTML: https://brahms.ircam.fr/fr/work/ma-mere-l%27oye. The performers, ages, date and venue are stated there; the premiere concerns the complete duet suite, not this recording.

cues.title: Letting the phrase finish
cues.text: The returning upper melody settles into longer notes. Ravel marks a slowing and a held final note, giving both players time to release the phrase together. Listen to the shared resonance after the last attacks rather than expecting a separate flourish from either player.
cues.evidence: Durand score, pp. 2–3, final Rall. and fermata. cache/analysis/ravel-ma-mere-loye-pavane.txt: detected attack density falls from about 1.4 per second at 85 seconds to 0.8 at 90 and 0.2 at 95; level falls to −19.4 dB at 95. The report supports the closing passage, not an exact release time.

transitions.title: The melody keeps going
transitions.how: The opening alternates a simple lower phrase with a higher, more decorated answer. The middle gives the upper line more continuous movement while the lower part sustains the harmonic support. The two players change their roles within a single piano sound; this is a change of texture and register, not an orchestral handover.
transitions.evidence: Durand score, pp. 2–3, bars 8–12: connected Prima line with reduced repeated accompaniment. The twenty-bar score and analysis boundary candidate at 38 seconds locate the middle approximately. No alignment file or exact bar time is claimed.

transitions.title: A familiar upper phrase returns
transitions.how: The high phrase heard earlier returns with its gently repeated accompaniment. Recognition comes from the melody and its register rather than a large change in volume. Ravel then lengthens the final gesture, adding a rallentando and a fermata so that the two parts can settle into one ending.
transitions.evidence: Durand score, p. 3, Prima bars 17–20 recalls bars 5–8, with a modified closing bar; final Rall. and fermata. Analysis has its strongest boundary candidate at 72 seconds and another at 78. The return is placed at passage level, not as a verified bar onset.

composer.background:
Ravel was born in Ciboure, across the harbour from Saint-Jean-de-Luz, to Marie Delouart, a Basque woman who had lived in Madrid, and Pierre-Joseph Ravel, a Swiss-born engineer. The family moved to Paris when Maurice was three months old. His father encouraged music as well as an interest in machinery; his mother’s songs gave him an early acquaintance with Spanish idioms. Basque ancestry and Spanish musical theatre remained distinct resources: the uneven pulse of the Piano Trio differs from the habanera of the Rapsodie espagnole. He returned to the Basque coast for holidays and composition, but received his musical education in Paris.

He entered the Conservatoire in 1889, initially as a pianist, and studied with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot. Failure to win the required prizes cost him his place in 1895. Readmitted in 1897 to Fauré’s composition class, he also learnt counterpoint from André Gedalge. Fauré encouraged the individual ear without relaxing the demands of construction; Gedalge supplied the discipline behind the fugues and independent inner parts. Ravel did not become a virtuoso pianist. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, introduced much of the difficult piano music, including Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit.
